# Schematic conventions

**Owner: Lance.** The KiCad project lives in `electricalDrawing/`.
`make hwcheck` must pass before any PR touching it is opened.

## Scope: schematic yes, PCB probably no

**Decision A.4 in `docs/DECISIONS.md`.** We capture the schematic; we do not fabricate a
board unless we take The Reach (handout §14).

A custom PCB earns **zero points** — the rubric grades mechanisms, measurements and the
soak — and adds fab turnaround on top of critical path B, which is already the thing most
likely to delay M2. A breadboard plus an off-the-shelf MCP2515 module clears every
guardrail, and the handout is explicit that the enclosure can be a food container.

The schematic is worth the time anyway, because three graded artifacts depend on it:

- `docs/DESIGN.md` needs an architecture diagram and a defensible wiring story
- `docs/hardware/wiring.md` needs pin assignments that cannot drift from reality
- The **three-isolated-workers test** needs a parts-only buyer who can order from the BOM
  without ever seeing the design

`electricalDrawing/electricalDrawing.kicad_pcb` stays in the repo, empty, on purpose — the
same way `src/capture/` does. Its emptiness is a recorded position, not an oversight.

## Sheet structure

Lance has blocked out functional areas on the root sheet. Keep that shape; it maps onto the
architecture, which makes both documents easier to defend:

| Block | Contains |
|---|---|
| **Power** | USB-C input from the car (switched, D-011) as an off-sheet connector, the Pi's 5 V rail, bulk and bypass caps. **No** OBD2 pin 16 and no buck converter. |
| **CAN** | OBD2 pin 6 / pin 14 / pin 5 via the Y-splitter, TJA1050 transceiver, MCP2515, crystal + load caps, termination jumper **drawn open** (D-011), `INT` to GPIO |
| **Pi interface** | 40-pin header, SPI0 (CE0/MISO/MOSI/SCLK), the interrupt GPIO, grounds |
| **Sensors** *(conditional, D-006)* | MPU-6050 on I2C with pull-ups; DS18B20 on 1-Wire with its 4.7 kΩ |

## Rules

1. **Every net that leaves a block is a named label**, not a wire crossing a boundary. The
   netlist is read by humans at the defense.
2. **Annotate the voltage domain on every power net** (`+5V_USB`, `+5V`, `+3V3`). The Pi has
   no 5 V-tolerant inputs and no over-voltage protection; a mislabeled rail is how a Pi dies
   silently in Week 13.
3. **Every IC gets its decoupling drawn**, even when the module already has it. The
   schematic documents what is *electrically true*, not what we happened to buy assembled.
4. **The MCP2515 crystal frequency is a value field, not a comment** — 8 MHz vs 16 MHz
   changes the device-tree overlay, and a wrong value produces a silently dead bus.
5. **No `DNP`/`no-connect` without a reason in the field.** Floating inputs are an ERC
   violation for good reasons.
6. **`make hwcheck` green before the PR.** ERC violations are build failures, exactly like
   `-Werror`.

## What must not be trusted to a datasheet alone

The cheap MCP2515 breakout modules vary: some run the TJA1050 at 5 V and level-shift the
controller side, and some do not — those drive **5 V onto MISO** and will kill a Pi.

**Meter it. With the Pi disconnected. Before anything is plugged in.** This is the exact
case `CLAUDE.md` §8.4 covers: no hardware conclusion from a verbal description or a
datasheet, on a board nobody has measured. Record the measured voltages in
`docs/hardware/wiring.md` with the date.

## Generated, never hand-edited

`make hwdocs` regenerates these from the schematic. If a pin table and the schematic
disagree, the schematic wins and the table was stale:

- `docs/figures/electricalDrawing.svg` — rendered schematic, **committed**, so pull requests
  show a picture instead of an S-expression diff
- `docs/hardware/bom.csv` — parts list feeding `BOM.md`
- `electricalDrawing/electricalDrawing.net` — netlist, the source for `wiring.md` pin tables

# Design document — carwatch

> **STATUS: M2 SKELETON.** 3–5 pages when complete. The handout calls these "the most
> leveraged hours of the whole project" — every hour of arguing here saves five of
> rewriting later.
>
> **Before submitting, run the three-isolated-workers check:** a design-only reviewer,
> a parts-only buyer who never sees the design, and a builder who only follows
> instructions must each succeed from their own section alone.

## 1. Architecture
> A diagram in the spirit of the handout's Figure 1: processes, threads, kernel
> components, data flows, **and rates on every arrow**. The rates are not decoration —
> they are what makes the mechanism justifications checkable.

```
  OBD2 port (Y-splitter, D-011)        car USB-C / 12 V socket (switched)
  pin 6 / 14 / 5                               │ 5.1 V ≥ 3 A → Pi
        │ CAN 500 kbit/s                       │ (cut, unannounced, at every key-off)
        ▼
  ┌──────────────┐  SPI0 @ [N] MHz     ┌────────────────┐
  │ MCP2515 +    │────────────────────▶│   candaemon    │  [mech B]
  │ TJA1050      │  INT ──▶ GPIO[N]    │  IRQ RX path   │
  │              │◀────────────────────│  Mode 01 req.  │  [N] req/s, D-012
  └──────────────┘  edge-triggered     └───────┬────────┘
     RX rate = responses + any port broadcast (pid-survey ATMA)
                                               │ SPSC ring, [N] frames/s  [mech F]
                                               │ shm, sequence-accounted
                    ┌──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
                    ▼                          ▼                      ▼
            ┌───────────────┐         ┌────────────────┐     ┌────────────────┐
            │   storaged    │         │   analyzed     │     │   obdctl       │
            │ append-only   │◀────────│ features →     │────▶│ query CLI      │
            │ CRC, fsync    │  read   │ baseline →     │ UDS │ 5 verbs        │
            │   [mech D]    │         │ model → FSM    │     └────────────────┘
            └───────────────┘         └───────┬────────┘     ┌────────────────┐
```

# Evaluation report — carwatch

> **STATUS: M5 SKELETON.** 3–4 pages. "Adjectives are not measurements."
> Claude can generate plausible code; it cannot fake your understanding of your own
> measurements — which is why the defense draws so heavily on this document. Every
> number in here must be one you can reproduce while someone watches.

## 1. Method and setup
Hardware, kernel version, build flags, what was running, how load was generated,
how many trials. Enough for a TA to re-measure.

**Every figure states whether its data is live, replay, or synth.** No exceptions.

## 2. Latency / timing
> Distributions, not just means. Under both idle and loaded CPU.

- CAN frame arrival → durable in the log: p50 / p95 / p99 / max, idle and loaded
- Histogram, not a table of means. [figure]

## 3. Resource footprint
> CPU and RSS per process, at steady state and **over the full soak**. The hourly
> heartbeats give you this series for free — plot it.

[figure: RSS vs. time, all processes, full 48 h]

A flat line here is the whole point. A device that leaks for 48 hours and happens not
to die has not passed the soak; it has outrun it.

## 4. Domain metric
> The one the product lives or dies by.

Detection accuracy against the ground truth we constructed: per-diagnostic confusion
matrix over the induced-fault fixtures, with the false-positive rate called out
separately because a monitor that cries wolf twice gets unplugged.

## 5. Fault-injection results
> For each failure mode in the design document's table: what we injected, what the
> system did, and **the log excerpt proving it**.

| Injected | Expected | Observed | Log excerpt |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sensor unplugged 10 min | | | |
| `kill -9 candaemon` | | | |
| Power cut mid-write | | | |
| Disk full | | | |

## 6. Mechanism comparisons
> Required by our menu choices. Present as experiments: method, data, conclusion.

### 6.1 Interrupt-driven vs. polling (mechanism B)
Method · data · conclusion. Include the CPU cost of the polling design at the rate
needed to match the interrupt design's drop rate — that comparison is the point.

### 6.2 No-drop ring under contention (mechanism F)
Sustained rate with sequence accounting proving zero drops, under `stress-ng`.

### 6.3 Crash consistency (mechanism D)
N power-cut trials, recovery outcome each time, bytes lost per trial.

## 7. Limitations
> Plainly. Closes the loop on the constraints and substitutions declared in docs/DESIGN.md §5.

"An honest limitations section is worth more at the defense than a suspiciously perfect
results section, and we notice which one we are reading."

Name at minimum: the fault classes we could not induce, what two vehicles cannot tell
us about a third, how long a baseline our window actually covers versus what the oil
trend deserves, and every place a number came from replay rather than live driving.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# carwatch

An always-on in-vehicle diagnostic recorder. It reads a car's own sensors off the CAN
bus, learns what *that specific car* looks like at each operating point, and reports
developing faults that a mileage sticker and a check-engine light both miss.

CS 370 Operating Systems term project — Camden Thomas & Lance Baron, Colorado State
University.

> **Status: M0 scaffolding.** Structure and contracts are in place; subsystems are
> stubs. See `docs/milestones.md`.

## What it does

| Diagnostic | Sensors that cooperate | Why a threshold can't do it |
|---|---|---|
| Oil pressure degradation across oil life | oil pressure + RPM + coolant temp | Oil pressure is a function of RPM and oil temperature. The signal is the *residual* after normalizing for both, trended over weeks. |
| Cooling system anomaly | coolant temp + ambient/intake temp + engine load | A short-cycling thermostat has a period and amplitude. A single temperature reading has neither. |
| Mixture drift (vacuum leak / failing O2 / dirty MAF) | short+long term fuel trim + MAP + RPM | Trim values are only meaningful relative to load; the diagnosis is which way trims move *as load changes*. |

## Hardware

See `docs/hardware/BOM.md` for the parts list and `docs/hardware/wiring.md` for the
pinout and the 3.3 V safety notes. Summary: Raspberry Pi 4, MCP2515 + TJA1050 CAN
module on SPI0 with `INT` on a GPIO, OBD2 pass-through Y-splitter (CAN_H pin 6, CAN_L
pin 14, signal ground pin 5). Power comes from the car's USB-C port or a 12 V-socket
USB-C adapter — no wiring into the car, nothing cut (decision D-011).

## Quick start (clean Raspberry Pi OS)

```sh
git clone <repo> && cd CS370-Term-Project
./scripts/provision_pi.sh      # packages, SPI overlay, user, service units
make                           # -Wall -Wextra -Werror clean
make test
sudo ./scripts/install.sh      # installs supervisor + daemons
obdctl status
```

Full TA-facing walkthrough is filled in at M4. **If the TA can't boot it, the TA can't
grade it** — this file is graded.

## Query interface

```
obdctl status                        # liveness, per-process RSS, event counts
obdctl verdicts [--since <when>]     # current and historical diagnoses
obdctl series <pid> --from --to      # raw or binned history
obdctl baseline <pid>                # the learned model for an operating-point bin
obdctl faults                        # detection/degradation/recovery events
```

**From a phone:** join the device's own Wi-Fi network (no internet — it has none) and open
its status page. The page is read-only and shows exactly `status` and `verdicts`; anything
deeper is `obdctl` (decision D-013).

## Repository layout

```
src/         systems core, C17, -Wall -Wextra -Werror clean
  common/    logging, time, config, error paths
  can/       MCP2515 SPI + interrupt RX path        [mechanism B]
  capture/   optional physical sensors (MPU-6050, DS18B20)
  ipc/       SPSC no-drop ring, UDS protocol        [mechanisms E, F]
  store/     append-only crash-consistent log       [mechanism D]
  analysis/  features, baselines, model, state machine
  supervisor/ watchdog, restart policy              [mechanism E]
  interface/ obdctl query CLI + read-only phone status page (D-013)
drivers/     out-of-tree kernel module (stretch, mechanism A)
tools/       PYTHON ALLOWED HERE ONLY — replay harness, training, plots,
             board_sync.py (reconciles docs/board.toml onto the GitHub board)
tests/       unit tests and fixtures
fixtures/    labeled captures, including induced faults
soak/        soak runner, heartbeat logs, fault injection
docs/        PROBLEM.md, DESIGN.md, EVALUATION.md (the three graded documents)
             board.toml (every task/question/decision) + BOARD.md (how it works)
             DECISIONS.md (audit log), PLAN.md (why the plan is shaped this way),
             milestones.md, handout/ (the rubric as markdown), hardware/
partners/    per-partner PROMPTLOG, REFLECTION, raw .jsonl transcripts
```

## The boundary

This product contains no LLM client, no cloud inference, and no third-party pretrained
model. The classifier weights in `models/` were trained by us from data we collected;
the training code is in `tools/train/`. The only network activity in the shipped tree
is serving the read-only status page on the device's own Wi-Fi access point, which has
no upstream connection. See `CLAUDE.md` §2.

body = '''
D-014. The supervisor is the only writer of GPIO17. Every live state blinks:

## What this changes It records the product form we settled on in the 2026-09-21 session and applies it across the repo. The device plugs into the **OBD2 port through a pass-through Y-splitter** for CAN data. It gets **power from the car's USB-C port** (or a 12 V-socket USB-C adapter) instead of OBD2 pin 16 plus a buck converter. It gets its signals from **rate-limited standard Mode 01 requests**. The owner reads it **from a phone over the device's own Wi-Fi** (read-only, no internet). There is **one warning light** on the box. The PR also records the Honda answer: **2015 Honda CR-V EX-L**. Nothing on either car is cut or spliced. Docs and board only: no C, no schematic, no scripts. ## Why We're building a prototype to prove the idea is worth something, not a finished product. But the product is something an ordinary owner plugs in, so the prototype installs the same way. Splicing CAN behind the port was rejected because those wires are the same conductors as pins 6 and 14. A camera-harness tap was rejected because a 2015 EX-L has no Honda Sensing camera. Full reasoning and rejected alternatives are in each decision entry. **Decision IDs touched:** D-007 (answered), D-011, D-012, D-013, D-014 (all new, all ⚠️ UNREVIEWED, all in the Review Queue) **Milestone:** M1 **Mechanism affected (B / D / E / F / none):** B (its *justification* now depends on port broadcast traffic, see D-012), D (power cut at every key-off is now literally true), E (the supervisor drives the warning light and supervises the status page) Closes: board item `productform`. Its issue number is not known yet, because `board_sync.py` cannot run on this machine (see Verification). ## Review this hardest 1. **D-012 → mechanism B.** D-002 justifies interrupts with a busy 500 kbit/s bus. If a car's port only answers our own requests, that justification fails for that car. I did **not** edit LOCKED §B.1. Instead, the PID survey now includes a 60 s `ATMA` capture, which decides whether a human reopens it. 2. **`keyoff` moved from M4 to M2 and now blocks `baseline`** (commit 2). Baseline data recorded on an undervolting USB supply is suspect, so the supply gets proven first. This puts one more item on critical path A. 3. **D-014 blink-only states.** A GPIO holds its last level when its writer dies, so a *steady* light, on or off, is defined to mean "not running". Check that this reasoning holds. ## What I am least sure about - **Whether this is one claim or four.** Each decision is its own commit so that any one of them can be reverted alone. But if Lance would approve D-011 and reject D-013, §7.5 says this PR should be split. I kept it as one PR because the decisions share the Review Queue table and CLAUDE.md §3, so separate PRs would conflict with each other. Lance, if you'd rather have them split, say so and I'll do it. - **Honda facts are inferred from the model year, not read off the car.** That covers the K24W engine, the CVT, no Honda Sensing on the EX-L, and an oil-pressure switch rather than a sender. `pidhonda` and the VIN are the evidence. - **Pi GND and OBD2 pin 5 reach chassis by two paths.** I expect that to be harmless. It is listed to be measured, not assumed. - **The ~10 requests/s Mode 01 budget** is an order-of-magnitude figure, deliberately left for DESIGN.md §4 to justify. ## Commit-by-commit 1. `95ec6f0` **D-007:** the Honda testbed is a 2015 CR-V EX-L. Includes the Maintenance Minder consequence for the memo. 2. `cb257d3` **D-011:** plugs in at the OBD2 port with a Y-splitter; power from the car's USB-C. The buck converter and pin 16 are gone; `keyoff` is rewritten and moved to M2. 3. `2f5d0be` **D-012:** rate-limited Mode 01 requests are the main data path, with a `--listen-only` flag. Adds the `ATMA` port check and new item `canreq`. 4. `5cf0e04` **D-013:** read-only phone status page over the device's own Wi-Fi. New item `phoneview`, first in the cut order. 5. `842252a` **D-014:** a warning light driven by the supervisor; every live state blinks. New item `led`. 6. `af5c810` Board item `productform`, which traces this PR. 481 changed lines across 11 files, all Markdown and TOML. Each decision is one commit, following the documentation rule in §7.3. The diffs are wide and shallow on purpose, so you can check that each decision was applied consistently everywhere it appears. ## Verification — paste real output, do not summarize **None of the gates could run on the authoring machine.** It has no `make` and no `gcc`, and its Python launcher points at a missing interpreter. This PR changes no C, so `make` and `make asan` can't be affected by it. `make test` can be, through `tools/test_board.py`, and **that is the one that must be run before merge.** The CI board workflow will run `--check --no-board` on this PR.

make asan ``` $ make asan /usr/bin/bash: line 1: make: command not found exit=127 ```

**Branch:** `camden/m1/product-topology`. Six commits, 481 lines, all Markdown and TOML. I didn't touch any C code, scripts, or `electricalDrawing/`.

| Commit | What it records |
|---|---|
| `95ec6f0` | **D-007:** the Honda is a 2015 CR-V EX-L. Adds the "Maintenance Minder already does this" objection to the memo task. |
| `cb257d3` | **D-011:** plugs into the OBD2 port through a Y-splitter; powered from the car's USB-C. The buck converter and OBD2 pin 16 are gone, and the wiring doc, parts list, schematic conventions and design doc are updated to match. |
| `2f5d0be` | **D-012:** the device polls standard Mode 01 PIDs (the ones every car must answer) at a limited rate, with a flag to send nothing. The PID survey now includes a 60 s `ATMA` check of port traffic. |
| `5cf0e04` | **D-013:** read-only phone page over the Pi's own Wi-Fi, showing status and verdicts only. `obdctl` stays the main interface; the page is first to be cut if M4 slips. |
| `842252a` | **D-014:** one LED, driven by the supervisor. Every working state blinks, so a steady light (on or off) always means "not running". |
| `af5c810` | A board item, `productform`, so the PR traces back to an issue. |

All five decisions are ⚠️ UNREVIEWED and listed in the Review Queue for Lance.

**Three calls I made on my own that you should check:**
1. **The USB power check moved from M4 to M2** and now has to pass before baseline collection starts. Baseline data recorded while the Pi is undervolting can't be trusted. The cost is one more item on the critical path.
2. **D-012 undercuts part of our case for mechanism B.** The argument for interrupts assumes a busy bus. If a car's port only answers our requests, that argument fails for that car. I didn't edit the locked entry (§B.1). The `ATMA` check decides whether you reopen it.
3. **It's one PR, not four.** The decisions share the Review Queue table and CLAUDE.md §3, so separate PRs would conflict. Each is its own commit and can be reverted alone. If Lance wants them split, I'll split them.

**Blockers:**
- **Python needs reinstalling.** Until it is, `make test` can't validate the board file and `board_sync.py` can't run. CI will probably show board drift on #83, because the four new items (`canreq`, `phoneview`, `led`, `productform`) aren't on GitHub yet.
- **I passed your commit identity on each command.** Git has no name or email configured here, so I used `CamdenThomas <camden.thomas@colostate.edu>`, copied from your earlier commits, without writing it into git config.

**Things I noticed but didn't touch** (each is separate work):
- `.kicad_prl` and `.history` are tracked in git, even though §7.12 forbids it.
- `make boundary` will flag the `socket()` calls that `src/ipc/` will need for its Unix sockets.
- `DESIGN.md` and `pid-survey.md` point to a `docs/decisions/` folder that doesn't exist.

**For M1:** the design your memo argues from is in place. When you write the memo's problem section, it needs to answer the Maintenance Minder objection. Still outstanding: the hardware order (#4) and the ELM327 surveys.

     1	# Problem memo — carwatch (Camden Thomas, Lance Baron)
     2	
     3	> **STATUS: M1 DRAFT.** One page maximum. Its job is to survive being read by a
     4	> skeptical stranger. Bracketed items are unfilled.
     5	
     6	## The user
     7	
     8	> Rubric: a person or place, **named or nameable**. "A cautious driver" is a persona and
     9	> will be returned for revision the same way "people who might want to monitor things"
    10	> would be. Name a human and a car.
    11	
    12	The typical american drives a substantial amount, releying heavily on thier vihicle. Many people drive previosly own vihivles with a wide viriaty if wear. People everyday are forced to rely on a car they hardly undestand just hoping the average service milestone will keep you car getiing you to work each day
    13	
    14	## The problem
    15	
    16	> Observable and costly: what goes wrong, how often, what it costs in money or worry.
    17	
    18	Maintenance intervals are generalizations. The sticker on the windshield knows nothing
    19	about how this engine has actually been run — a commuter that never reaches operating
    20	temperature and a highway car with the same odometer reading have not aged the same
    21	way. The consequence runs both directions and both are expensive: oil changed far
    22	earlier than it needed to be, or an engine run on oil that lost its pressure margin
    23	weeks ago. While the sensors already present do a great job tracking all the need information,
    24	people just need a device to monitor and store this data to learn the car and predict failures before the check engine light of doom puts you on the hour long bus ride.
    25	
    26	## Why a device
    27	
    28	> The 3 a.m. test: why must something be physically present and always awake? And why
    29	> doesn't a phone app already solve this?
    30	
    31	The signal is a slow trend across weeks of driving, and it is only interpretable if you
    32	have the cold starts, the short trips, and the long pulls — *all* of them, not the
    33	drives someone remembered to open an app for. A phone app is present for the trips you
    34	thought to instrument, which is a biased sample of exactly the variable being measured.
    35	
    36	The interesting moment is also never the moment anyone is looking: it is the third cold
    37	start of a February week where warm-up took ninety seconds longer than it did in
    38	January. Nobody is holding a phone then. The device is in the car, awake at key-on,
    39	recording before anyone has decided anything is wrong.
    40	
    41	And the data stays in the car. No account, no upload, no fleet telematics company
    42	holding a log of everywhere this person drove.
    43	
    44	## The sensors
    45	
    46	> Which two (or more) and how they **cooperate** rather than coexist.
    47	
    48	The vehicle's own sensors, read via the OBD2 port: oil pressure, coolant temperature,
    49	intake air temperature, MAP, O2 / fuel trims, RPM, engine load.
    50	
    51	They cooperate because **no one of them means anything alone.** Oil pressure is a
    52	function of RPM and oil temperature; the diagnostic signal is the *residual* after
    53	normalizing for both, which requires all three sensors to reach one conclusion. Fuel
    54	trim is only interpretable against load. Coolant temperature only indicts a thermostat
    55	once ambient temperature and load have been accounted for. Every verdict this device
    56	produces requires at least two sensors to agree on something a single threshold cannot
    57	see.
    58	
    59	## The mechanisms
    60	
    61	> First guess at two menu items, one sentence of justification each. May change by M2.
    62	
    63	**B — interrupt-driven input with a polling comparison.** At 500 kbit/s the MCP2515's
    64	two receive buffers overflow in milliseconds, so a poll loop either burns a core or
    65	loses frames; the `INT` line lets us service the controller only when it has something.
    66	
    67	**D — custom append-only storage with crash consistency.** The power is cut mid-write
    68	every single time the key turns off, so the storage layer never gets a clean shutdown
    69	and must recover a torn tail on every boot.
    70	
    71	## The risk
    72	
    73	> The single thing most likely to sink this project. Name it now.
    74	
    75	the trends such as oil life needs a real viscosisty interval to develop, and that is calendar time we cannot buy back by working harder in Week 14. While there will be clear structure for a data logger, the ML model likely will not be able to demonstrate any real worl predictions on the model car (2015, Honda, CRV). Likely a fake obd2 port will need to be made to provide constant data for both training the diagnostic ML model and to perform the full 48 hour soak test, as we can not drive a car or run a car for 48 hours

    51	They cooperate because **no one of them means anything alone.** Oil pressure is a
    52	function of RPM and oil temperature; the diagnostic signal is the *residual* after
    53	normalizing for both, which requires all three sensors to reach one conclusion. Fuel
    54	trim is only interpretable against load. Coolant temperature only indicts a thermostat

    56	produces requires at least two sensors to agree on something a single threshold cannot
    57	see.

####
# CI for the project board (CLAUDE.md 7.11, docs/BOARD.md).
#
# Two guarantees, one workflow:
#   manifest - docs/board.toml is well-formed (offline, always fast)
#   drift    - GitHub actually matches it, i.e. nobody forgot to run sync
#
# plus a third, soft for now: every PR traces back to an issue.
####
name: board

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read
  issues: read

jobs:
  manifest:
    name: board.toml is well-formed
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: python tools/test_board.py

  drift:
    name: GitHub matches board.toml
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      # --no-board keeps this inside GITHUB_TOKEN's reach: user-level Projects
      # need a PAT, issues do not. The board follows from the issues anyway.
      # --check exits 1 when anything would change.
      - name: board_sync --check
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        run: python tools/board_sync.py --check --no-board

  pr-closes-issue:
    name: PR traces back to an issue
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # SOFT LAUNCH. Failing red on your own PRs while you are still learning the
    # flow teaches you to bypass the check, which is the opposite of the point.
    # Delete this line once the habit is set - target 2026-09-26.
    continue-on-error: true
    steps:
      - name: body must contain "Closes #<n>"
        env:
          BODY: ${{ github.event.pull_request.body }}
        run: |
          if printf '%s' "$BODY" | grep -Eiq '(close[sd]?|fix(e[sd])?|resolve[sd]?)[[:space:]]+#[0-9]+'; then
            echo "ok - PR closes an issue"
          else
            echo "::error::PR body has no 'Closes #<n>'. CLAUDE.md 7.11: every PR traces back to an issue; if there is no issue, add the [[item]] to docs/board.toml first."
            exit 1
          fi

####
# CI for the project board (CLAUDE.md 7.11, docs/BOARD.md).
#
# Two guarantees, one workflow:
#   manifest - docs/board.toml is well-formed (offline, always fast)
#   drift    - GitHub actually matches it, i.e. nobody forgot to run sync
#
# plus a third, soft for now: every PR traces back to an issue.
####
name: board

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read
  issues: read

jobs:
  manifest:
    name: board.toml is well-formed
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: python tools/test_board.py

  drift:
    name: GitHub matches board.toml
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      # --no-board keeps this inside GITHUB_TOKEN's reach: user-level Projects
      # need a PAT, issues do not. The board follows from the issues anyway.
      # --check exits 1 when anything would change.
      - name: board_sync --check
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        run: python tools/board_sync.py --check --no-board

  pr-closes-issue:
    name: PR traces back to an issue
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # SOFT LAUNCH. Failing red on your own PRs while you are still learning the
    # flow teaches you to bypass the check, which is the opposite of the point.
    # Delete this line once the habit is set - target 2026-09-26.
    continue-on-error: true
    steps:
      - name: body must contain "Closes #<n>"
        env:
          BODY: ${{ github.event.pull_request.body }}
        run: |
          if printf '%s' "$BODY" | grep -Eiq '(close[sd]?|fix(e[sd])?|resolve[sd]?)[[:space:]]+#[0-9]+'; then
            echo "ok - PR closes an issue"
          else
            echo "::error::PR body has no 'Closes #<n>'. CLAUDE.md 7.11: every PR traces back to an issue; if there is no issue, add the [[item]] to docs/board.toml first."
            exit 1
          fi

=================== src/capture/README.md
# src/capture — physical sensors on the Pi

**Empty on purpose.** This directory exists because decision **D-006** is open: if the
48-hour soak must run on live sensors, an MPU-6050 and a DS18B20 land here and the
architecture is already shaped to receive them (they push into the same SPSC ring that
`candaemon` uses, so nothing downstream changes).

Do not delete this directory. Its emptiness is a documented design position, not an
oversight.
=================== soak/README.md
# soak/ — the 48-hour unattended run

The handout requires the logs to show, at minimum:

1. A timestamped startup.
2. A heartbeat **at least hourly** recording process liveness, resident memory (RSS),
   and cumulative event counts.
3. **At least one injected fault** during the run — physically unplug a sensor for ten
   minutes, or `kill -9` a sensor process — with detection, degradation, and recovery
   visible in the log.
4. An orderly state at the end.

Raw, unedited logs are the graded deliverable. **Do not tidy them.** Real systems are
never that tidy, and a cleaned soak log is the artifact this course is best equipped to
notice.

## Before the graded run

Start soak-style overnight runs at small scale from **M3**, not M4. Every leak found in
Week 9 is a crisis avoided in Week 14. `make soakcheck` runs a one-hour miniature.

Leave margin to run the graded soak **twice**. You will want to.

## Open: what the soak runs against

See **D-006**. Until it closes, build as if live sensors are required.
=================== soak/run_soak.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Soak runner. --mini runs a 1-hour rehearsal (make soakcheck); default is the real 48h.
set -euo pipefail

DURATION=$((48 * 3600))
LABEL="soak"
if [[ "${1:-}" == "--mini" ]]; then DURATION=3600; LABEL="mini"; fi

STAMP="$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"
LOGDIR="soak/logs/${LABEL}-${STAMP}"

## 3. The Guardrails: What "Non-Trivial" Means Here

An open-ended project needs a floor, or the path of least resistance becomes a Python
script that polls a sensor and prints a number. Five guardrails define the floor.
Everything above them is yours.

### 3.1 Two sensors that cooperate

Your device must incorporate **at least two physically distinct sensors**, and they must
**cooperate**: fused into one decision, correlated against each other, or feeding a single
shared pipeline whose behavior depends on both. Two independent demos stapled together at
the README do not satisfy this requirement. That's one sensor short of the assignment,
twice. Cooperation is also where the systems content hides. Two sensors almost never want
the same sampling rate, the same interface, or the same latency budget, and reconciling
those differences inside one program is the first real design problem this project hands
you.

### 3.2 Below the application layer: the mechanism menu

Your system must include **at least two** of the following mechanisms, implemented by you,
identified explicitly in your design document, and measured in your evaluation. This is the
guardrail that keeps the project an operating-systems project rather than a wiring
exercise.

| # | Mechanism | What "measured" means |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | A kernel module or character driver for one of your sensors, exposing it via `/dev` or sysfs | Correct concurrent access; behavior under load; a clean `dmesg` |
| **B** | Interrupt-driven input, with a head-to-head comparison against a polling design | Event latency distribution and CPU utilization, both ways |
| **C** | Real-time scheduling (`SCHED_FIFO`/`SCHED_RR`) for a latency-critical path | Jitter and deadline-miss rate vs. the default scheduler, under load |
| **D** | A custom storage layer: ring buffer, append-only log, or small FUSE filesystem, with an explicit crash-consistency story | Write batching and `fsync` discipline; recovery after a mid-write power cut |
| **E** | A multi-process architecture: sensors isolated in separate processes, a hub aggregating over IPC (shared memory, message queues, or Unix domain sockets), a supervisor that survives any child dying | Kill any child at any time; the system degrades, logs, recovers |
| **F** | A high-rate sampling pipeline with a no-drop guarantee: lock-free or single-producer/single-consumer ring between capture and consumption | Sustained rate with zero drops, proven by sequence accounting, under CPU contention |

Choose the two (or more) that **your problem demands**, not the two that look easiest. The
design document (Section 8) requires you to justify each choice from the user's
requirements, and the defense will test that justification. Figure 1 shows where these
mechanisms live in a reference architecture.

repeatedly and in roughly this order, what can:

- **Substitute.** Downgrade the sensor; keep the problem. A PIR and a door switch see more
  of a household's rhythm than you'd guess a thermal camera was needed for. A microphone's
  RMS level is a serviceable occupancy proxy. And two cheap sensors that corroborate each
  other routinely outperform one expensive one standing alone. Notice that "corroborate each
  other" is Section 3.1 arriving early, wearing a budget. Record in the design document what
  you wanted, what you used, and what the substitution costs in capability.

- **Make your own ground truth.** You can't wait for the bearing to fail, so you provoke the
  conditions and label the recordings: the taped washer, the loosened bolt, the greenhouse
  vent propped open on purpose, a one-week paper logbook of real door events. **Ten labeled
  recordings you made are worth more than ten thousand unlabeled samples you found**,
  because you know what yours mean. And at the defense, you will be asked how you know.

- **Replay.** Build a harness that feeds recorded sensor streams through your real pipeline

1	/* Single-producer / single-consumer lock-free ring — mechanism F.
     2	 *
     3	 * The no-drop guarantee is the point. A gap in the record is a gap in the diagnosis,
     4	 * so a drop must be impossible to hide: every slot carries a sequence number and the
     5	 * consumer accounts for every one of them. If the ring is full the producer must
     6	 * report the overrun rather than silently overwrite an unread sample (D-002).
     7	 *
     8	 * Layout is fixed so the ring can live in shared memory across the process boundary
     9	 * that mechanism E requires.
    10	 */
    11	#ifndef CARWATCH_RING_H
    12	#define CARWATCH_RING_H
    13	
    14	#include <stdatomic.h>
    15	#include <stdbool.h>
    16	#include <stddef.h>
    17	#include <stdint.h>
    18	
    19	#define RING_CAPACITY 4096u   /* power of two — the mask depends on it */
    20	#define RING_PAYLOAD    16u   /* bytes; one CAN frame's data field fits with room */
    21	
    22	typedef struct {
    23	    uint64_t seq;                    /* monotonic, never reused */
    24	    uint64_t mono_ns;                /* CLOCK_MONOTONIC at capture */
    25	    uint32_t can_id;
    26	    uint8_t  len;
    27	    uint8_t  src;                    /* data_src_t — live | replay | synth */
    28	    uint8_t  _pad[2];
    29	    uint8_t  data[RING_PAYLOAD];
    30	} ring_slot_t;
    31	
    32	typedef struct {
    33	    _Atomic uint64_t head;           /* producer writes */
    34	    _Atomic uint64_t tail;           /* consumer writes */
    35	    _Atomic uint64_t overruns;       /* refused pushes — must stay zero */
    36	    uint64_t         _pad[5];        /* keep head/tail off one cache line */
    37	    ring_slot_t      slot[RING_CAPACITY];
    38	} ring_t;
    39	
    40	void     ring_init(ring_t *r);
    41	
    42	/* Returns false when full. Never overwrites an unread slot; increments overruns. */
    43	bool     ring_push(ring_t *r, const ring_slot_t *in);
    44	
    45	/* Returns false when empty. */
    46	bool     ring_pop(ring_t *r, ring_slot_t *out);
    47	
    48	uint64_t ring_overruns(const ring_t *r);
    49	size_t   ring_depth(const ring_t *r);
    50	
    51	#endif

entries.name: EnterPlanMode
entries.description:
Use this tool proactively when you're about to start a non-trivial implementation task. Getting user sign-off on your approach before writing code prevents wasted effort and ensures alignment. This tool transitions you into plan mode where you can explore the codebase and design an implementation approach for user approval.

## When to Use This Tool

**Prefer using EnterPlanMode** for implementation tasks unless they're simple. Use it when ANY of these conditions apply:

1. **New Feature Implementation**: Adding meaningful new functionality
   - Example: "Add a logout button" - where should it go? What should happen on click?
   - Example: "Add form validation" - what rules? What error messages?

2. **Multiple Valid Approaches**: The task can be solved in several different ways
   - Example: "Add caching to the API" - could use Redis, in-memory, file-based, etc.
   - Example: "Improve performance" - many optimization strategies possible

3. **Code Modifications**: Changes that affect existing behavior or structure
   - Example: "Update the login flow" - what exactly should change?
   - Example: "Refactor this component" - what's the target architecture?

4. **Architectural Decisions**: The task requires choosing between patterns or technologies
   - Example: "Add real-time updates" - WebSockets vs SSE vs polling
   - Example: "Implement state management" - Redux vs Context vs custom solution

5. **Multi-File Changes**: The task will likely touch more than 2-3 files
   - Example: "Refactor the authentication system"
   - Example: "Add a new API endpoint with tests"

6. **Unclear Requirements**: You need to explore before understanding the full scope
   - Example: "Make the app faster" - need to profile and identify bottlenecks
   - Example: "Fix the bug in checkout" - need to investigate root cause

7. **User Preferences Matter**: The implementation could reasonably go multiple ways
   - If you would use AskUserQuestion to clarify the approach, use EnterPlanMode instead
   - Plan mode lets you explore first, then present options with context

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Only skip EnterPlanMode for simple tasks:
- Single-line or few-line fixes (typos, obvious bugs, small tweaks)
- Adding a single function with clear requirements
- Tasks where the user has given very specific, detailed instructions
- Pure research/exploration tasks (use the Agent tool instead)

## What Happens in Plan Mode

In plan mode, you'll:
1. Thoroughly explore the codebase using Glob, Grep, and Read
2. Understand existing patterns and architecture
3. Design an implementation approach
4. Present your plan to the user for approval
5. Use AskUserQuestion if you need to clarify approaches
6. Exit plan mode with ExitPlanMode when ready to implement

## Examples

### GOOD - Use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Add user authentication to the app"
- Requires architectural decisions (session vs JWT, where to store tokens, middleware structure)

User: "Optimize the database queries"
- Multiple approaches possible, need to profile first, significant impact

User: "Implement dark mode"
- Architectural decision on theme system, affects many components

User: "Add a delete button to the user profile"
- Seems simple but involves: where to place it, confirmation dialog, API call, error handling, state updates

User: "Update the error handling in the API"
- Affects multiple files, user should approve the approach

### BAD - Don't use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Fix the typo in the README"
- Straightforward, no planning needed

User: "Add a console.log to debug this function"
- Simple, obvious implementation

User: "What files handle routing?"
- Research task, not implementation planning

## Important Notes

- This tool REQUIRES user approval - they must consent to entering plan mode
- If unsure whether to use it, err on the side of planning - it's better to get alignment upfront than to redo work
- Users appreciate being consulted before significant changes are made to their codebase

entries.name: ExitPlanMode
entries.description:
Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan to the plan file and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode system message
- This tool does NOT take the plan content as a parameter - it will read the plan from the file you wrote
- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve
- The user will see the contents of your plan file when they review it

## When to Use This Tool
IMPORTANT: Only use this tool when the task requires planning the implementation steps of a task that requires writing code. For research tasks where you're gathering information, searching files, reading files or in general trying to understand the codebase - do NOT use this tool.

## Before Using This Tool
Ensure your plan is complete and unambiguous:
- If you have unresolved questions about requirements or approach, use AskUserQuestion first (in earlier phases)
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval

**Important:** Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan okay?" or "Should I proceed?" - that's exactly what THIS tool does. ExitPlanMode inherently requests user approval of your plan.

## Examples

1. Initial task: "Search for and understand the implementation of vim mode in the codebase" - Do not use the exit plan mode tool because you are not planning the implementation steps of a task.
2. Initial task: "Help me implement yank mode for vim" - Use the exit plan mode tool after you have finished planning the implementation steps of the task.
3. Initial task: "Add a new feature to handle user authentication" - If unsure about auth method (OAuth, JWT, etc.), use AskUserQuestion first, then use exit plan mode tool after clarifying the approach.

You should build your plan incrementally by writing to or editing this file. NOTE that this is the only file you are allowed to edit - other than this you are only allowed to take READ-ONLY actions.

## Plan Workflow

### Phase 1: Initial Understanding
Goal: Gain a comprehensive understanding of the user's request by reading through code and asking them questions. Critical: In this phase you should only use the Explore subagent type.

1. Focus on understanding the user's request and the code associated with their request. Actively search for existing functions, utilities, and patterns that can be reused — avoid proposing new code when suitable implementations already exist.

2. **Launch up to 3 Explore agents IN PARALLEL** (single message, multiple tool calls) to efficiently explore the codebase.
   - Use 1 agent when the task is isolated to known files, the user provided specific file paths, or you're making a small targeted change.
   - Use multiple agents when: the scope is uncertain, multiple areas of the codebase are involved, or you need to understand existing patterns before planning.
   - Quality over quantity - 3 agents maximum, but you should try to use the minimum number of agents necessary (usually just 1)
   - If using multiple agents: Provide each agent with a specific search focus or area to explore. Example: One agent searches for existing implementations, another explores related components, a third investigating testing patterns

### Phase 2: Design
Goal: Design an implementation approach.

Launch Plan agent(s) to design the implementation based on the user's intent and your exploration results from Phase 1.

You can launch up to 1 agent(s) in parallel.

**Guidelines:**
- **Default**: Launch at least 1 Plan agent for most tasks - it helps validate your understanding and consider alternatives
- **Skip agents**: Only for truly trivial tasks (typo fixes, single-line changes, simple renames)

In the agent prompt:
- Provide comprehensive background context from Phase 1 exploration including filenames and code path traces
- Describe requirements and constraints
- Request a detailed implementation plan

### Phase 3: Review
Goal: Review the plan(s) from Phase 2 and ensure alignment with the user's intentions.
1. Read the critical files you identified during exploration to deepen your understanding
2. Ensure that the plans align with the user's original request
3. Use AskUserQuestion to clarify any remaining questions with the user

### Phase 4: Final Plan
Goal: Write your final plan to the plan file (the only file you can edit).
- Begin with a **Context** section: explain why this change is being made — the problem or need it addresses, what prompted it, and the intended outcome
- Include only your recommended approach, not all alternatives
- Ensure that the plan file is concise enough to scan quickly, but detailed enough to execute effectively
- Name the critical files to be modified. For changes that repeat a pattern across many files, describe the pattern once and list a few representative paths — do not enumerate every file or line number
- Reference existing functions and utilities you found that should be reused, with their file paths
- Include a verification section describing how to test the changes end-to-end (run the code, use MCP tools, run tests)

### Phase 5: Call ExitPlanMode
At the very end of your turn, once you have asked the user questions and are happy with your final plan file - you should always call ExitPlanMode to indicate to the user that you are done planning.
This is critical - your turn should only end with either using the AskUserQuestion tool OR calling ExitPlanMode. Do not stop unless it's for these 2 reasons

**Important:** Use AskUserQuestion ONLY to clarify requirements or choose between approaches. Use ExitPlanMode to request plan approval. Do NOT ask about plan approval in any other way - no text questions, no AskUserQuestion. Phrases like "Is this plan okay?", "Should I proceed?", "How does this plan look?", "Any changes before we start?", or similar MUST use ExitPlanMode.

NOTE: At any point in time through this workflow you should feel free to ask the user questions or clarifications using the AskUserQuestion tool. Don't make large assumptions about user intent. The goal is to present a well researched plan to the user, and tie any loose ends before implementation begins.
</system-reminder>

# Plan — repo overhaul to the USB-OBD2, CR-V-only design

## Context

Camden's new PROBLEM.md draft, plus his answers this session, move the project a long way:
- **Data path:** a USB OBD2 adapter (ELM327/STN chip) replaces the MCP2515. Raw CAN becomes a stretch goal only.
- **Vehicles:** one car, the 2015 Honda CR-V. The Subaru is dropped.
- **Soak and training data:** a "fake OBD2 port" feeds both, because no car can run for 48 h.
- **Scope of edits:** `electricalDrawing/` stays untouched for Lance. PROBLEM.md gets stale-only edits.

Most of the repo still describes MCP2515/SPI/CAN, two cars, and placeholder directories. The goal: no stale information, no empty staging directories, and a layout a stranger can navigate from one index.

**A correction to the question I asked you.** Handout §3.2 defines F as a *high-rate* pipeline. Mode 01 through a USB adapter gives about 10–20 samples/s and no burst. So without CAN, only **D and E** hold up on their own. B and F come back only if the Pi gets a sensor of its own; that goes on the board as a decision.

## Branches

- **PR A:** `camden/m1/repo-overhaul`, stacked on `camden/m1/product-topology` (#83), stated in the PR body. Docs, board, scripts and directory layout only.
- **PR B:** `camden/m1/obd-rename`, stacked on A. Contains the C and Makefile changes. **It stays a draft**, because this machine has no gcc/make/WSL and CLAUDE.md requires pasted `make`/`make test`/`make asan` output.

Decisions stay in the same commit as their propagation (§7.3). New decisions are ⚠️ UNREVIEWED and go in the Review Queue. Replaced LOCKED decisions move to DECISIONS §G with pointers and are never deleted.

## PR A — commits, in order

**0. Camden's own work, committed as-is (3 commits, one per file)**
- The PROBLEM.md draft.
- The milestones.md M0 check-offs.
- PROMPTLOG E-02.

My edits come after, so the history shows which words are yours.

**1. D-015: a USB OBD2 adapter replaces the MCP2515; CAN is a stretch goal**
- **DECISIONS:**
  - Move A.1/D-001 to §G, pointing at D-015.
  - Revise the unreviewed D-011 (data half) and D-012 in place: drop the CAN IDs, the `ATMA` check, and the B-consequence text.
- **Hardware docs:**
  - Rewrite `docs/hardware/wiring.md`: adapter, USB-C power, LED.
  - Rewrite `BOM.md`: adapter in; the MCP2515 moves to a "Stretch" table.
  - Strip the `ATMA` section from `pid-survey.md`.
- **Other docs:** DESIGN §1/§3/§5, README hardware, CLAUDE.md §3/§8.4 examples, PLAN critical path B, and the milestones exit criteria (M1 stretch, M2 "electrically alive").
- **Scripts and tools:** rewrite `scripts/provision_pi.sh` (no SPI overlay; a udev symlink `/dev/obd`) and update the `tools/pidscan.py` docstring.
- **PR template:** replace the "candump excerpt" wording.
- **Board:**
  - Retitle `bench`, `firstcap` and `canreq` to the adapter path.
  - Cut `twonode` and `meterv` (status done plus a cut note, per the PLAN §3 rule).
  - Update the `order` and `pidhonda` bodies.

**2. D-016: the CR-V is the only testbed**
- Move A.2/D-005 to §G.
- Fix every "both vehicles/cars" and Outback reference: CLAUDE.md §3, DECISIONS E.2, PLAN §1/§3 (the second car was cut #1; remove that line), milestones, the pid-survey column.
- Board: cut `pidsub`, and update the `baseline`, `foil`, `fvac`, `oilq` and `memo` bodies.

**3. D-017: commit to mechanisms D + E; B and F depend on a Pi-side sensor**
- Move B.1/D-002 to §G.
- Update CLAUDE.md §4, DESIGN §2/§6, and EVALUATION §2/§6.
- The PROBLEM.md mechanisms paragraph is your only memo line I touch. It's stale MCP2515 text; I replace it with D and E.
- Board:
  - Mark `canirq`, `canpoll` and `expirq` contingent.
  - Add decision item **`pisensor`** (M2, camden): a DS18B20 or MPU-6050 on the Pi. It addresses three things:
    - It settles the §3.1 "two physically distinct sensors" risk, which one USB device makes worse.
    - It gives the soak a live sensor.
    - It restores B and F.

- Rewrite E.3 (still OPEN).
- Move the email text into the body of board item `soakq`, and delete `docs/professor-email-draft.md`.
- Add task **`obdsim`** (M3): `tools/obdsim.py`, an ELM327 emulator on a pty, with all output labeled `synth`.
- Update `tools/README.md` (replace `cangen.py` with `obdsim.py`).

**5. Record Camden's M0 check-offs**
- D-008: dates verified. Update F.3 and the `dates` body; closing it needs a human `--close-questions`.
- `cleanup` → status done.

**6. Process docs match CLAUDE.md §7.3/§7.5**
- `.gitmessage`: remove the stale "≤3 files / ≤150 lines" caps, and update the area list.
- PR template: fix the stale caps line.
- DECISIONS F.1: add a pointer saying the line caps are superseded by CLAUDE.md §7.3.
- Delete `.github/pull_request_template_note.md`. The ruleset is done and recorded in `ghsetup`.

**7. Remove placeholder directories**
- Delete every `.gitkeep`: docs/figures, fixtures, models, soak, both transcripts dirs, and src/capture.
- Delete `src/capture/` entirely.
- Drop `!models/.gitkeep` from .gitignore.
- Change the partners READMEs' copy-out to `mkdir -p … && cp`.
- Remove references to `drivers/`, `src/capture/`, and `cangen.py`.

**8. Add `docs/README.md`: a library index**
- One table: every doc, what it answers, whether it's graded, who owns it, and whether it's generated.
- Link it from the root README's repository-layout section. The layout listing itself is rewritten to match the tree.

## PR B — draft, unverified until built on the Pi or WSL
- `git mv src/can src/obd`; `candaemon` → `obdd` in the Makefile, CLAUDE.md §6/§7.4, README, DESIGN, DECISIONS F.2, and `.gitmessage`.
- `ring_slot_t.can_id` → `pid` (`include/ipc/ring.h`, plus `tests/test_ring.c` if it's used there), and fix the payload comment.
- `REC_CAN_FRAME` → `REC_OBD_RAW` in `include/store/record.h`. That file is Lance's, so this PR is `[cross]`.
- Rewrite the `src/obd/main.c` header comment for the tty path.

## Not touched
- `electricalDrawing/`, `docs/hardware/schematic-conventions.md`, D-009/D-010, and the KiCad board items (`schpower`, `schcan`, `schpi`, `symlib`, `hwgate`). These are Lance's; I flag the staleness in the PR.
- `docs/handout/`, `board.lock.json` (generated), and PROMPTLOG E-01.
- Your PROBLEM.md prose. I list issues back to you instead:
  - The user section is a persona.
  - "Predict failures" contradicts the narrow claim in E.1.
  - A soak on a fake port conflicts with the handout.
  - Typos.

## Verification
- `python tools/test_board.py`: must PASS; paste the output.
- `python tools/board_sync.py --check`: read-only; paste the drift report.
- Stale-term sweep: `git grep -n -i -E "\bcan\b|MCP2515|SPI|candaemon|candump|Subaru|Outback|both (cars|vehicles)"`. The only allowed hits are stretch-goal mentions, DECISIONS §G, the handout, Lance's KiCad docs, and PROMPTLOG history.
- `git ls-files | grep gitkeep` returns nothing; no tracked directory is empty.
- `make`/`make test`/`make asan` can't run here (no toolchain). PR A has no C changes. PR B stays a draft until the output is pasted.
- At session end, `python tools/board_sync.py` pushes the board. Cut items labeled `hardware` (`twonode`, `meterv`, `pidsub`) need a human `--close-questions`, and I'll report that rather than bypass it.
- Your formatting edits to the *generated* milestones table will be overwritten on the next sync. That's expected; the real fix would be in `board_sync.py`.

55	## A.1 — CAN reaches the Pi via MCP2515 on SPI, not Bluetooth 🔒
56	`D-001` · Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
57	
58	**Decision.** The Pi reads raw CAN frames through an MCP2515 + TJA1050 module on SPI0,
59	with the controller's `INT` line on a GPIO for edge-triggered receive. Not a Bluetooth
60	ELM327 dongle.
61	
62	**Why.** A Bluetooth ELM327 hands us parsed ASCII over a userspace socket at a few
63	samples per second. With no interrupt line, no SPI transaction and no bus-level timing,
64	mechanisms **A, B, C and F all become unavailable** — and the handout requires at least
65	two mechanisms implemented by us, below the application layer. The MCP2515 path keeps
66	the kernel boundary inside our repository, where it is graded. It is also better for the
67	user: raw bus access sees frames the ELM327 protocol never exposes, at the rate the ECU
68	publishes them rather than the rate a request/response dongle can poll.
69	
70	**Cost.** More wiring, a 3.3 V/5 V level question to get right, one-time decode work per
71	vehicle. Accepted.
72	
73	**Consequences.** `src/can/` owns SPI transactions and the IRQ path (Camden). The
74	interrupt-vs-polling comparison is a first-class deliverable, not an afterthought. A
75	Bluetooth ELM327 may appear in `tools/` as a cross-check; it may never be the product's
76	path.

175	## A.6 — Plug-in form: OBD2 port for data, car USB-C for power ⚠️ UNREVIEWED
176	`D-011` · Decided M1, 2026-09-21 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
177	
178	**Decision.** The device is a box anyone could install without tools:
179	- **Data:** a Y-splitter (pass-through) cable at the OBD2 port — CAN_H pin 6, CAN_L pin 14,
180	  signal ground pin 5 — into the MCP2515 module. The port stays usable for a scan tool
181	  or an emissions inspection.
182	- **Power:** the car's own USB-C port, or a USB-C adapter in the 12 V socket, into the Pi.
183	  **OBD2 pin 16 is not used.** The 12 V→5 V buck converter leaves the BOM.
184	- **Nothing is cut, spliced, pierced or clamped** on either car.
185	
186	**Why.** The product thesis is that this is a thing an ordinary owner plugs in, so the
187	prototype is built the way the product would be installed. We are building the model to
188	prove the idea is worth something, not the finished product — but a prototype that needs
189	harness surgery proves a different, less interesting idea. Switched USB power also means
190	no battery drain while parked, and it makes mechanism D's defining constraint literally
191	true: power is cut, unannounced, at every key-off.
192	
193	**Alternatives rejected** (discussed 2026-09-21):
194	- *Splice CAN_H/CAN_L behind the OBD2 port.* The wires behind the port are the same
195	  conductors as pins 6 and 14 — same traffic, plus a cut harness on a daily driver. If a
196	  gateway were filtering the port, a splice there would not get past it either.
197	- *In-line harness at the forward camera.* Not available: the 2015 CR-V EX-L has no Honda
198	  Sensing camera (D-007).
199	- *Contactless (inductive) CAN clamp.* Receive-only, a black box between the bus and our
200	  code, and it needs a wiring diagram to find the pair.
201	- *OBD2 pin 16 + our own buck converter.* Live with the key off (battery drain), and more
202	  hardware to build and defend.
203	
204	**Rules this imposes** (also in `docs/hardware/wiring.md`):
205	1. **Remove the module's 120 Ω termination jumper.** The car's bus is already terminated;
206	   ours would drop it to ~40 Ω.
207	2. **Keep the stub short** — the Y-cable plus module leads under ~0.3 m at 500 kbit/s.
208	3. **The Pi must not brown out at crank.** Adapter rated ≥ 5.1 V / 3 A (Pi 4). Proven by
209	   `vcgencmd get_throttled` after a cold start, not by the adapter's label.
210	
211	**Cost.**
212	- No recording while the key is off — nothing happens then worth recording, but the device
213	  also cannot run overnight in a parked car.
214	- D-006 option (c), the parked-car soak, now requires a socket that stays live in
215	  accessory plus a battery tender.
216	- USB ground and OBD2 signal ground both reach chassis by different paths. Expected to be

218	- The CAN side still needs a physical cable to the port; the product is "one box, two

221	## A.7 — Standard Mode 01 requests are the primary data path ⚠️ UNREVIEWED
222	`D-012` · Decided M1, 2026-09-21 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
223	
224	**Decision.** `candaemon` gets its signals by sending **standard OBD2 Mode 01 requests** at
225	a fixed, rate-limited schedule (functional request ID `0x7DF`, responses `0x7E8`–`0x7EF`,
226	one request outstanding at a time). Manufacturer broadcast frames are recorded when the
227	port carries them and used where decoded, but **nothing depends on them.** A
228	`--listen-only` build flag puts the MCP2515 in listen-only mode and sends nothing.
229	
230	**Why.** D-011 makes this a plug-in device, and the thing that makes a plug-in device work
231	on a car it has never seen is the part of the protocol every car must speak. Mode 01 over
232	CAN is mandatory on US cars from model year 2008; manufacturer frames differ per make, per
233	model, often per year. This also matches D-005's existing mitigation — "start on standard
234	Mode 01 PIDs only". *"Learns this car's normal"* is precisely what lets one device serve
235	different cars without per-model decode work: it never needs to know what normal *is*
236	ahead of time.
237	
238	**Sample-rate consequence.** Signals are round-robined, so each PID is sampled at
239	(request rate ÷ PID count) — on the order of 1 Hz each for a ~10 requests/s budget over
240	~8 PIDs. That is ample for what we diagnose (oil trend over weeks, warm-up over minutes,
241	fuel trim against load) and must be stated in `docs/DESIGN.md` §4. The request budget itself
242	is a design-doc number to justify, not a constant to pick.
243	
244	**Consequence for mechanism B — to check, not assumed.** D-002's case for interrupts is a
245	busy 500 kbit/s bus overflowing the MCP2515's two buffers in milliseconds. That holds only
246	if the port carries **broadcast** traffic. If a car's port is silent except for our own
247	responses, B's *commitment* stands but its *justification* on that car does not. The PID
248	survey now includes a 60 s `ATMA` capture at the port for exactly this
249	(`docs/hardware/pid-survey.md`). If both ports are quiet, B.1's justification is reopened
250	with a human — not quietly rewritten.
251	
252	**Cost.** The device now transmits on a daily driver's bus. Kept safe by the rate limit,
253	one outstanding request, and only standard requests; the listen-only flag is the fallback
254	if either owner objects.
255	
256	**Scope note.** "Works on any car" is the product's direction, not our claim. The claim is
257	still E.1: three faults, two cars, measured error rates.

261	# B. Systems architecture and mechanisms
262	
263	## B.1 — Mechanism commitments: B, D, E, F 🔒
264	`D-002` · Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
265	
266	The handout requires two. We commit four and will measure all of them.
267	
268	**B — interrupt-driven input with a polling comparison.** `src/can/`. At 500 kbit/s a busy
269	bus delivers a frame roughly every 230 µs; the MCP2515's two receive buffers overflow in
270	milliseconds. A poll loop either burns a core or drops frames. Measured as event-latency
271	distribution and CPU, both ways, idle and loaded.
272	
273	**D — custom append-only storage, crash-consistent.** `src/store/`. *The defining
274	constraint: power is cut mid-write every time the key turns off.* We never get a clean
275	shutdown. Measured by pulling power mid-write, repeatedly, and proving recovery.
276	
277	**E — multi-process with a supervisor.** `src/supervisor/`, `src/ipc/`. A recorder that
278	dies silently has actively harmed its user, who believes it is on duty. Any child may be
279	`kill -9`'d; the system degrades, logs, recovers.
280	
281	**F — no-drop SPSC ring, sequence-accounted.** `src/ipc/ring.c`. Key-on produces a burst;
282	a gap in the record is a gap in the diagnosis. Measured as sustained rate with zero drops
283	under contention.
284	
285	**Stretch, M4+ only:** **A** (character driver for the MCP2515) and **C** (`SCHED_FIFO` on
286	the capture path). Do not start either until B, D, E and F are implemented *and measured*.
287	A half-finished kernel module is worth zero points and costs two weeks.
288	
289	## B.2 — Four processes, not one 🔒
290	`D-002` (corollary) · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
291	
292	`candaemon`, `storaged`, `analyzed` and `supervisor` are separate processes with separate
293	address spaces, communicating over a shared-memory ring and Unix domain sockets.
294	
295	**Why.** Fault isolation is the product requirement, not an architectural preference: the
296	analysis engine is the most complex and least trustworthy component, and it must not be
297	able to take the capture path down with it. One process would be simpler and would fail
298	the thing the device exists to do.
299	
300	## B.3 — The ring refuses rather than overwrites 🔒
301	Decided M0 · **By:** Claude, from D-002 · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
302	
303	When the ring is full the producer returns failure and increments an overrun counter. It
304	does **not** overwrite the oldest unread slot.
305	
306	**Why.** Overwriting loses data silently, and silent loss is the exact failure mechanism F
307	exists to make impossible. A refusal is visible, countable, and reportable; an overwrite
308	looks like a quiet minute. Enforced by `tests/test_ring.c`.
309	
310	**Reviewer note.** This is a real trade: under sustained overload we drop *new* data
311	rather than *old*. If that is ever the wrong choice for a diagnostic, reopen this.
312

345	## B.5 — One warning light, driven by the supervisor ⚠️ UNREVIEWED
346	`D-014` · Decided M1, 2026-09-21 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
347	
348	**Decision.** One LED on a GPIO (proposed GPIO17, header pin 11, through 330 Ω), written
349	**only by the supervisor**. Every state in which the device is working is a *blink
350	pattern*:
351	
352	| Light | Meaning | Priority |
353	|---|---|---|
354	| fast blink (~4 Hz) | **degraded** — a child is down, CAN silent while the engine runs, storage failing, or undervoltage | highest |
355	| double-blink, pause | **a verdict has surfaced** (after D.3 hysteresis and dwell) — look at the phone | |
356	| slow blink (~1 Hz) | on duty, recording, nothing to report | lowest |
357	| **steady on or steady off** | **the device is not running.** Never a valid state. | — |
358	
359	**Why a light at all.** The 3 a.m. test: nobody is looking at a phone at the moment that
360	matters. It also makes "honest reporting through our own interface" (demo movement 1)
361	visible from across the room when a sensor is unplugged.
362	
363	**Why every live state blinks.** A GPIO keeps its last level after the process driving it
364	dies. If "verdict" were solid-on, a crashed supervisor would freeze the light into a false
365	alarm, or into a false all-clear if it froze off. With blink-only states, a stuck light of
366	either kind can only mean *not running*. This is D-002's principle — a recorder that dies
367	silently has harmed its user — applied to the one output a driver actually sees.
368	
369	**Why the supervisor, not `analyzed`.** The supervisor already knows every child's
370	liveness (mechanism E), so it can show "degraded" when `analyzed` itself has died; a light
371	owned by `analyzed` would show a stale verdict instead. Verdicts reach the supervisor over
372	the existing UDS. One writer, no GPIO contention.
373	
374	**Cost.** One more thing the supervisor does, and one more thing it must not block on: the
375	blink timer must never delay `waitpid` handling. Colour, brightness and placement are open
376	(M4 enclosure).

380	# C. Storage and data integrity
381	
382	## C.1 — Append-only, self-framing, CRC'd records 🔒
383	`D-002/D` · Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
384	
385	Records are never rewritten in place. Each carries a magic number for resynchronization
386	and a CRC32 over its whole body. Recovery scans from the last known-good offset, verifies
387	CRCs, truncates the torn tail, and logs exactly what was lost.
388	
389	**Why.** We are interrupted mid-write by design, several times a day. Rewriting in place
390	can destroy data that was previously correct; appending can only ever damage the last
391	record. The CRC is what makes a torn record *detectable* rather than merely wrong — and
392	wrong numbers you trust are more dangerous than missing numbers you know about.
393	
394	**Open sub-decision (M2, Lance):** fsync batch size and interval. There is no correct
395	value, only one justifiable from user requirements. Document the argument in `docs/DESIGN.md`
396	§4 before writing the code.
397	
398	## C.2 — Every record carries a provenance tag 🔒
399	Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
400	
401	Every record and every log line carries `src = live | replay | synth`. Present in the
402	format from day one, before any replay tooling exists.
403	
404	**Why.** Handout §5: replayed or synthesized data must be labeled everywhere it appears —
405	logs, report, demo. Making it a mandatory field rather than a convention means it is
406	structurally impossible to forget. Mislabeling synthesized data as live is the single
407	integrity failure this course is best equipped to detect, and the worst trade available
408	anywhere in it.
